source.book: The Art and Science of Technical Analysis
source.author: Adam Grimes
source.chapter_title: The Market Cycle and the Four Trades

conventions: stop and limit entries mechanized as bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; price-level conditions rejected (shift test)

candidates.name: AccumulationDistributionRangeContext
candidates.quote: prices move sideways in a trading range bounded by rough areas of support and resistance, an intermediate-term moving average is flat, and price chops back and forth on both sides of that moving average... Eventually, higher prices will bring increased supply into the market, balance is achieved, and prices will stop rising.
candidates.description: Defines two of the cycle's four phases precisely enough to test: a market is in a sideways range (recent range width tight relative to volatility) with a flat intermediate-term moving average that price repeatedly crosses. Whether that range is accumulation (base before a markup, long context) or distribution (top before a markdown, short context) is distinguished by the direction of the swing structure leading into the range: a prior decline precedes accumulation, a prior advance precedes distribution.
candidates.pseudocode:
rangeWidth = highest(high, rangeLookback) - lowest(low, rangeLookback)
isTight = rangeWidth <= tightMultiple * atr(atrLookback)
emaSlope = ema(close, emaLength) - ema(close, emaLength)[emaSlopeLag]
isFlat = abs(emaSlope) <= flatSlopeAtrFraction * atr(atrLookback)
priorTrendDown = close[rangeLookback] < close[rangeLookback + priorTrendLookback]
accumulationContext = isTight AND isFlat AND priorTrendDown

complexity.reason: 'flat', 'tight', and 'prior trend direction' each need a numeric design decision Grimes does not supply; distinguishing accumulation from distribution mechanically also requires deciding how far back to look for the prior trend

notes: This is the phase-1/phase-3 definition of Wyckoff's four-phase cycle (accumulation, markup, distribution, markdown), which is the chapter's central framework per the mining brief's steering.

candidates.name: MarkupMarkdownTrendPhase
candidates.quote: Markup: The classic uptrend... Markdown: The downtrend that follows distribution.
candidates.description: Defines the other two cycle phases: markup is a sustained series of higher swing highs and higher swing lows (mirrored: markdown is lower swing highs and lower swing lows). The classic with-trend-legs-and-pullbacks structure Grimes references here ('a series of with-trend legs interspersed with pullbacks') is developed fully in Chapter 3 (mined separately); this candidate is the cycle-level phase test.
candidates.pseudocode: lastSwingHigh(1) > lastSwingHigh(2) AND lastSwingLow(1) > lastSwingLow(2)  // uses G01-01 pivot detection

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection (G01-01) and comparison of the two most recent pivot pairs

candidates.name: SpringUpthrustFailureTest
candidates.quote: The most common of these is what Wyckoff called a spring, which is called a failure test at the bottom of the range in modern terminology... Candles with long shadows extending below support but with few or no closes below that support are a sign of accumulation... This pattern is the opposite of the Wyckoff spring, and is usually called an upthrust.
candidates.description: The named support-holding pattern for the accumulation phase and its mirror for distribution: a spring is a bar whose low probes below the recent range's low (a stop run / liquidity test) but whose close finishes back at or above that level, showing the probe was immediately rejected; an upthrust is the mirror at the top of the range, a pop above resistance that fails to hold.
candidates.pseudocode:
rangeLow = lowest(low[1], rangeLookback)
spring = low[0] < rangeLow - marginAtrFraction * atr(atrLookback) AND close[0] >= rangeLow

complexity.reason: a window-min/max lookup plus a margin and a close comparison, no cross-bar persistent state

notes: Grimes's own description is qualitative ('few or no closes below support' over a span of bars, and that intrabar excursions below support typically last less than a quarter of the bar's own timeframe on a lower time frame -- an unobservable-from-this-timeframe detail, so only the single-bar close-back-inside form is mechanized here). This is the pattern the mining brief explicitly names ('springs', 'upthrusts') as a support/resistance-holding candidate.

candidates.name: TrendContinuationPullbackContext
candidates.quote: Perhaps the most common trend continuation play is to use the pullbacks in a trend to position for further trend legs.
candidates.description: The trend-continuation trade category's framework-level definition: an entry with the trend (G02-02) taken on a pullback. The precise pullback structure (simple vs. complex, depth as a fraction of the prior swing, first pullback after a breakout) is left to Chapter 3 (mined separately); this candidate records only the cycle-level statement that ties the trade category to the phase.
candidates.pseudocode: MarkupMarkdownTrendPhase(...) AND isPullback(...)  // isPullback left abstract, defined precisely in Chapter 3

complexity.reason: depends on both a trend definition and a pullback definition, neither given a precise numeric form in this chapter

notes: Kept for completeness per the mining brief's instruction to define each of the four trades precisely; the actual pullback mechanics are expected from Chapter 3's mining pass, and the dedup pass should treat this as a coarse duplicate of whatever specific pullback-entry rules that chapter produces.

candidates.name: TrendContinuationRiskAtSwingInvalidation
candidates.quote: The key to defining risk is to define the points at which the trend trade is conclusively wrong, at which the trend is violated.
candidates.description: The stop for a trend-continuation trade sits beyond the swing point (the pullback low in an uptrend / pullback high in a downtrend) that defined the entry -- the point at which the trend thesis is falsified.
candidates.book_order_type: stop beyond the invalidating swing point, mechanized as close-then-next-open

complexity.reason: reads a swing/pivot level established at or before entry and tracked across the position's life

candidates.name: TrendTerminationOverextensionFade
candidates.quote: a trader might find spots where the rallies in the uptrend have run up too far too fast, and take short positions against those rallies, planning to cover one to three bars later.
candidates.description: A fast countertrend scalp: within an established uptrend, short a rally that has advanced an unusually large amount in a short number of bars (overextended), planning a very short holding period. Mirrored for a plunge within a downtrend (buy the oversold spike). Grimes gives no numeric definition of 'too far too fast' in this chapter.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (assumed market order at the close, i.e. next-open per convention)

complexity.reason: 'too far too fast' has no numeric threshold in this chapter; a design decision is needed for both the lookback and the magnitude

notes: Grimes explicitly warns this is 'for only the fastest and most nimble traders' and that 'developing traders are well advised to avoid these countertrend scalps' -- kept per the high-recall instruction, not because it is recommended.

candidates.name: CoverOverextensionFadeAfterFixedBars
candidates.quote: planning to cover one to three bars later.
candidates.description: The trend-termination overextension scalp (G02-06) is covered after a small, fixed number of bars regardless of profit.
candidates.book_order_type: time-based exit at the next open once the bar count is reached
notes: Grimes's number is one to three bars; the existing NumBars rule's default (50) should be overridden to this range for this specific placement.

candidates.name: SupportRangeBounceEntry
candidates.quote: It is easy to find examples of well-defined trading ranges on historical charts where you could buy and risk a very small amount as the market bounces off the magic price at the bottom of the range.
candidates.description: The support/resistance-holding trade: buy near the low of an identified, well-defined trading range, with a small stop just beyond the range low. Grimes cautions this is only the cleanest subset of support-holding trades and that support usually does not hold this cleanly in practice (see G02-03 spring for the more common, messier form).
candidates.pseudocode:
rangeLow = lowest(low[1], rangeLookback)
close[0] <= rangeLow + proximityAtrFraction * atr(atrLookback) AND close[0] > rangeLow
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (assumed market/limit at close-then-next-open per convention)

complexity.reason: a rolling lowest-low is a crude proxy for what Grimes means by a genuinely 'well-defined' range; real range-boundary identification needs pivot/structure detection, not just a fixed window minimum

candidates.name: HigherLowsIntoResistancePrecedeBreakoutTrade
candidates.quote: The best resistance breaking trades will be driven by large-scale buying imbalances, and these imbalances usually show, for instance, as the market holds higher lows into the resistance level before the actual breakout.
candidates.description: Context filter for the support/resistance-breaking (breakout) trade category: a run of successive higher pivot lows pressing against a stable resistance ceiling precedes the best breakouts. Mirrored for lower highs pressing into a support floor before a breakdown.
candidates.pseudocode: pivotLow[k] > pivotLow[k+1] for k = 0..(numHigherLows-1) AND highest(high, rangeLookback) is roughly flat over that span

complexity.reason: needs pivot detection plus counting a rising sequence of pivot lows and a check that the resistance ceiling is stable

notes: Same underlying pattern as G01-05 (Chapter 1's Figure 1.10 preview of this idea); the dedup pass should merge the two -- this file's version ties it explicitly to the support/resistance-breaking trade category, which Chapter 1 only previewed.

chapter_summary: This chapter is the market-cycle framework: Wyckoff's four phases (accumulation, markup, distribution, markdown) and the four trade categories (trend continuation, trend termination, support/resistance holding, support/resistance failing), which the mining brief flags as central and to be defined cleanly since later chapters build on them. G02-01/G02-02 give the phase definitions (research/hard grade, since 'flat', 'tight', and trend direction all need design decisions); G02-03 mechanizes the named spring/upthrust failure-test pattern; G02-04 through G02-09 cover the four trades, each tied back to a phase or a pivot primitive, with trend continuation (G02-04/G02-05) explicitly deferred to Chapter 3's pullback taxonomy and the higher-lows-into-resistance breakout setup (G02-09) duplicating G01-05 from Chapter 1 -- the dedup pass should merge those two. Most of the rest of the chapter is Wyckoff crowd-psychology narrative (smart money vs. public, mania, media coverage) with no bar-level content, recorded as rejects.
